title: Real-World Applications of GitHub Actions
learning_outcomes: Explain the key behavior of real-world applications of github actions and identify when it should be used.
Configure or review the workflow fields and permissions relevant to real-world applications of github actions.
Verify the result using a controlled run or static check and interpret the evidence.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on real-world applications of github actions. Workflows can validate pull requests, test and build applications, generate documentation, publish packages or images, and deploy applications. Use the example to predict the workflow result, then verify the behavior in a safe test repository or by static review.
content.why_it_matters: Real-World Applications of GitHub Actions matters because it affects correctness, security, maintainability, or operating cost. Workflows can validate pull requests, test and build applications, generate documentation, publish packages or images, and deploy applications. Treat the workflow as an event-driven automation graph: an event starts the run, jobs are scheduled, steps execute on runners, and the run records a result.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Workflows can validate pull requests, test and build applications, generate documentation, publish packages or images, and deploy applications. Treat the workflow as an event-driven automation graph: an event starts the run, jobs are scheduled, steps execute on runners, and the run records a result. The most useful check is one that produces observable evidence and fails clearly when its stated requirement is not met.

items.title: Pull request validation
items.text: Match the event to the intended lifecycle, then test positive and negative branch/path/activity cases. Event payloads may be attacker-controlled, and scheduled jobs use UTC rather than a guaranteed exact start time.

items.title: Automated testing and builds
items.text: Make the check deterministic and fail with a meaningful status when requirements are not met. Preserve reports where useful and configure required branch checks to match the checks the workflow actually emits.

items.title: Documentation generation
items.text: For documentation generation, state the expected input and result, identify the relevant workflow field or operational decision, and verify it with a controlled check plus run logs. Document the failure condition rather than relying on the YAML file merely parsing.

items.title: Package publishing
items.text: Trace the release to a source commit, validate the selected version/ref, restrict publication permissions, retain build evidence, and verify the published artifact before promoting it.

items.title: Container image publishing
items.text: Build and identify an image deterministically, grant only required registry permissions, scan/verify before promotion, and prefer immutable digests or traceable tags over mutable “latest” references.

items.title: Website and application deployment
items.text: For website and application deployment, state the expected input and result, identify the relevant workflow field or operational decision, and verify it with a controlled check plus run logs. Document the failure condition rather than relying on the YAML file merely parsing.

content_blocks.code:
name: Build and retain output
on: workflow_dispatch
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: mkdir -p dist && echo "sample build output" > dist/README.txt
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: sample-build
          path: dist/
content_blocks.expected_output: The run uploads the generated `dist/README.txt` file as the `sample-build` artifact.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Start it manually in a test repository, then open the run summary and download the artifact to confirm the path.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Delete the sample workflow and any downloaded test artifact when finished.

content_blocks.title: Practice and verification
content_blocks.text: Inspect the example and make one focused change related to real-world applications of github actions. Predict the expected result first, then use the run instructions or a static review to check it. Record the difference between your prediction and the actual result. Do not add production secrets or grant write permissions just to make a sample pass.

items.title: Syntax and scope
items.text: Check YAML indentation and confirm whether the setting belongs at workflow, job, or step level.

items.title: Permissions and trust
items.text: Start with read-only access. If the example needs more access, explain the exact operation and reduce permissions again afterwards.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Use the run summary and first failing step. A green result is meaningful only when the intended checks actually ran.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain real-world applications of github actions, read the example, and identify a way to validate it. The wider system goal remains: Understand why automation belongs beside source control and how events become repeatable work.

content.task: Apply real-world applications of github actions to a small workflow change. State the expected result first, validate the configuration, then record evidence from the run or static check.
task_acceptance_criteria: Identify the relevant event, workflow field, runner behavior, or security boundary.
Explain the expected success result and at least one failure or skip condition.
Use least privilege and a disposable/test context; do not include credentials or production resources.
hints: Start with the key behavior: Workflows can validate pull requests, test and build applications, generate documentation, publish packages or images, and deploy applications.
Inspect the exact event filters, permissions, expressions, inputs, and job dependencies that affect this example.
Compare the observed status and logs with the expected result; distinguish static validation from a real hosted run.
content.expected_output: The expected result is the behavior described here: Workflows can validate pull requests, test and build applications, generate documentation, publish packages or images, and deploy applications. The real result depends on the repository, selected ref, configured permissions, and runner availability.
troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.
summary: Workflows can validate pull requests, test and build applications, generate documentation, publish packages or images, and deploy applications.
Treat the workflow as an event-driven automation graph: an event starts the run, jobs are scheduled, steps execute on runners, and the run records a result.
Use the provided example as a starting point, replace placeholders with repository-specific checks, and validate both success and expected failure behavior before publication.
